prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat bands at magic twist angles in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B009 as a single-part prize with the three supplied names. The decisive point for me is the structure the prize is meant to recognise. There is a specific, falsifiable prediction (the 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model of flat bands at a magic angle) and an original experiment that tested it (the 2018 correlated-insulator and superconducting-dome measurements from Jarillo-Herrero's group). Nobody could previously reach this regime, and the twist angle is now a tuning knob that has opened a field across van der Waals materials. The basic phase diagram has been reproduced by many independent groups using transport and scanning-probe methods, which is the experimental verification I insist on. Round 1 also showed that the trio is the most agreed credit on the shortlist: all eight members' preferred configurations use exactly these names where B009 appears, and every B009 supporter would keep Bistritzer. I would word the citation around the flat bands and the correlated insulating and superconducting states as observed phenomena, and not around a pairing mechanism, so that the open mechanism question is not something the committee has to resolve.
statement.case_against: The attribution gap is real and the three-name limit does not close it. Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto identified reduced bandwidth in twisted bilayers before 2011, and Cao, Fatemi and other co-first authors did the hands-on 2018 work. I have not checked the primary literature myself, and I would rather say that than pretend otherwise. Twist-angle disorder and sample-to-sample variation also make parts of the superconductivity claim soft, so a purist can call recognition early. Finally, B049 is a mature, cleanly attributed, well-verified alternative with strong atomic-physics support, and if the committee concludes the B009 credit cannot be drawn defensibly, B049 is the configuration I could support, provided the citation is narrowed to the magic-wavelength lattice.

responses.point: Lindroth places the lattice clock first because the clock result is more complete than twisted bilayer graphene in both interpretation and attribution, and calls the early theory and the co-first authors attribution problems that three names cannot fix. She also argues that Katori's magic-wavelength idea is a real conceptual step, not a refinement.
responses.response: Your argument on the clock moved me on one point. Trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength is a distinct idea, not simply a better comb or ion clock, and as an instrument person I accept that it solves a real problem that single ions cannot. I did not give that enough weight in round 1, and it is why B049 stays my first alternative. I do not agree that the graphene case is incomplete in the same sense. What the prize should recognise is the original prediction and the original experiment, and both are in the record. The pairing mechanism is a question about what comes after the door opens, and the clock's own interpretive questions (the redefinition of the second has not happened) are also still prospective. On attribution, I would say the Lopes dos Santos work is about a reduced Fermi velocity at small angles, whereas the magic-angle condition and the flat-band construction that the experiments tested is Bistritzer-MacDonald, though I repeat that the committee should check this against the papers. I also note that your own reservation about Lemonde, Hollberg and NIST priority has the same shape as mine for graphene, so neither candidate escapes an attribution question.

responses.point: Kroll answered my novelty question by saying the 2005 prize honoured the comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems, while the lattice clock interrogates 1e3 to 1e5 atoms where the trap does not shift the clock transition, and he would keep Ye's comb work out of the citation.
responses.response: That is a useful answer and I accept most of it. If the citation rests on the magic-wavelength lattice and the performance it enabled, the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is much smaller than I implied, and I withdraw the suggestion that the clock is merely a refinement of an honoured lineage. I keep one distinction. A prize for the original experiment has to say who first showed a lattice clock, and neither of us has verified that history, so I would want Katori's first demonstration and the NIST and SYRTE work dated from the primary papers before the committee votes. You also disclosed your year in Hall's laboratory in the JILA group where Ye works. I do not think that disqualifies your judgment, and I think the committee should simply note it. My position remains that B009 is the more original opening of new territory, but I would no longer call the clock a lesser case, only one I rank second.

responses.point: As Chair, Pearce moved to B049 largely on the judgment of atomic-physics colleagues and treats that as a limit on his own confidence. He argues that, because I ranked the clock second, B049 is a serious compromise acceptable to both camps.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour about your confidence, and I agree that two named members across fields rating B049 highly is meaningful. But I do not want the vote to be decided by who finds a candidate acceptable second. That is a count, not a scientific judgment, and you said yourself you are not trying to manufacture consensus. My ranking of the clock second reflects that I think it is a valid prize, not that I would trade the graphene discovery for it. The evidence that would move me is specific: if the primary literature showed that the magic-angle prediction was in substance already made before 2011, or that the 2018 discovery could not be credited to Jarillo-Herrero's group without naming Cao, then I would move to B049. Absent that, I stay with B009. Because you asked for primary-literature checks, I suggest we split them: the committee checks both candidates against the original papers and not just against our memories.

responses.point: Eriksson supports keeping the Bistritzer name and would word the citation around the prediction and discovery rather than around individuals, while acknowledging that Cao's role in the 2018 papers is a real difficulty.
responses.response: I agree with your wording approach and with keeping the trio. A principled reading of the rules is that we credit the decisive contribution at the level of the group's leader and the theorists whose model made the prediction, and that the students' hands-on work is exactly the credit gap the three-name limit forces on us in many past prizes. I do not think it is a reason to withhold a prize that the science supports. I would still put it on the record in our public discussion that Cao and Fatemi did the experiment, because the record should not suggest otherwise.

uncertainties: Whether the primary literature supports crediting Bistritzer and MacDonald over Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto for the magic-angle prediction. I have not verified this and am relying on memory and colleagues.
Whether the committee can defend omitting Cao, Fatemi and other co-first authors and Cory Dean's group within three names. This is the point most likely to change my position.
Whether the superconducting dome is settled enough to appear in the citation, or whether the correlated insulator is the safer anchor.
Who first demonstrated the lattice clock and whether Lemonde, Hollberg and NIST colleagues have a claim that makes a two-name B049 prize incomplete.
Whether a two-part prize is feasible at all. B049 uses two names and B009 uses three, so a combination exceeds the limit of three unique people, and I treat them as competing single-part options.
statement.conflict_note: I have no known collaboration with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, nor with Katori or Ye. Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague and Mehlig is in the neighbouring GU department. Chalmers has superconducting-circuit activity relevant to B040, which I do not prefer. I have used no disclosure from other members to change my position, but I note Kroll's year in the JILA group and Johansson's closeness to the B040 groups.
